name: Hot-sauce thermogenics / spicy food

lead: Some dieters add hot sauce, chilies or capsaicin supplements hoping to speed metabolism and trim body fat for a leaner look.

Capsaicin activates the TRPV1 heat receptor on sensory nerves, and proponents say this raises heat production and lowers appetite. Reviews cited on Wikipedia found no direct link between capsaicin and weight loss, and a 2014 meta-analysis reported weak evidence that capsaicin before a meal might slightly reduce intake.

paras: People eat spicy food with meals, use hot sauce as a low-calorie flavour, or take capsaicin capsules as a supplement. It is typically an add-on to a calorie-controlled diet, not a standalone method, and any effect reported is small.

Capsaicin can irritate the mouth, stomach, skin and eyes, causing nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain or diarrhea at large amounts. Isolated case reports link concentrated pills or extreme spicy challenges to serious events including cardiac problems. People with reflux or ulcers may find it worsens symptoms.

angle.text: Forum posters eat chili and hot sauce, or take capsaicin supplements, to speed metabolism and trim body fat for a leaner look. Capsaicin triggers a heat response that proponents say lifts energy use and curbs appetite. Reviews have found small effects on food intake and no direct link to weight loss.

lead: Hot-sauce thermogenics refers to eating chili peppers, hot sauce or capsaicin supplements in the belief that the heat raises metabolism or curbs appetite and so helps people get leaner. Leanness shows up in the face and the physique, which is why spicy-food diets appear in fat-loss and body-composition conversations. Capsaicin, the pungent compound in chilies, binds the TRPV1 receptor on pain-sensing nerves, producing sensations of heat [1].

Wikipedia reports that a 2007 source found no evidence linking capsaicin ingestion directly to weight loss, and that a 2014 meta-analysis found weak evidence that capsaicin before a meal might slightly reduce intake [1]. A 2022 umbrella review of eleven systematic reviews and meta-analyses concluded the overall health effect of spicy food and chili peppers is unclear, reporting associations with some cancers alongside inverse associations with metabolism, mortality and cardiovascular disease outcomes [2].

Dermatology reviews list spicy food among the commonly reported triggers of facial flushing in rosacea [3][4], and gastroenterology reviews note that spicy food is frequently reported to worsen reflux symptoms [5]. Large doses of capsaicin can irritate and cause nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain [1].
infobox: Raised metabolism, reduced appetite, fat loss
Weak evidence of a slight reduction in intake when taken before a meal [1]
Spicy food is a commonly reported rosacea flushing trigger [4]

paras: Capsaicin opens the TRPV1 ion channel on nociceptor nerve fibres, causing warmth and sometimes stinging; research on these sensors was recognised by the 2021 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine [1]. Orally it is well absorbed but extensively metabolised in the liver, with a blood half-life of about 25 minutes after a pepper extract in humans [1].

Wikipedia notes that well-designed trials have been hard to run because pungency makes doses difficult for participants to tolerate [1]. The 2014 meta-analysis suggested a small possible effect on food intake and a shift toward carbohydrate preference [1].

The 2022 umbrella review pooled eleven systematic reviews and meta-analyses covering 27 findings in humans. It reported direct associations with esophageal, gastric and gallbladder cancers and negative associations with metabolism-related outcomes, mortality and cardiovascular disease, and described consumption as typically safe while calling for higher-quality evidence [2]. A 2023 review notes that spicy food is frequently reported to worsen reflux but that hard evidence linking it to objective reflux is lacking [5].

Rosacea reviews list spicy food, alcohol and hot drinks among the most frequently reported triggers of flushing and symptom flares, though results vary between subtypes and advice to patients has been inconsistent [4][3]. Facial redness is one of the ways diet can affect how the face looks.

Capsaicin irritates skin, eyes and airways, and peppers are among the common plant exposures reported to poison centres [1]. A 2012 case report described a heart attack in a healthy 25-year-old after cayenne pepper pills, and a 2024 autopsy linked a teenager's death to a spicy chip challenge [1].

No studies found specific to hot sauce as a fat-loss or appearance aid. Studies of capsaicin itself reported weak evidence of a small effect on food intake [1], and an umbrella review of observational and trial syntheses on spicy food and chili peppers found the overall health effect unclear [2].

lore.intro: Spicy food is occasionally linked on looksmax.org to masculinity and testosterone, with members treating tolerance for heat as a sign of high testosterone [6].
